title: At-least-once, in practice
sub: A visibility timeout expires on a slow worker. What happens to the side effect?

frames.caption: A queue holds one message: charge order 42. Two workers, A and B, poll it. Visibility timeout: 30 seconds.
Worker A receives the message. The queue does not delete it; it hides it for 30 seconds, waiting for A to confirm it is done.
A is slow: a long garbage-collection pause, or a slow payment API. 30 seconds pass without A deleting the message, so the queue assumes A died and makes it visible again.
Worker B receives the same message and starts processing it too. Neither worker did anything wrong: this is what at-least-once delivery means.
Both finish and both charge the card. The customer is billed twice. A plain consumer turns every redelivery into a duplicate side effect.
A queue holds one message: charge order 42. Two workers, A and B, poll it. Visibility timeout: 30 seconds.
Worker A receives the message. The queue does not delete it; it hides it for 30 seconds, waiting for A to confirm it is done.
A is slow: a long garbage-collection pause, or a slow payment API. 30 seconds pass without A deleting the message, so the queue assumes A died and makes it visible again.
Worker B receives the same message and starts processing it too. Neither worker did anything wrong: this is what at-least-once delivery means.
Now the consumer is idempotent: in the same database transaction as the charge, it records 'processed #42'. A commits first.
B tries to do the same and finds #42 already recorded (a unique-key conflict), so it skips the charge and just deletes the message. One charge, however many deliveries: effectively-exactly-once.
